items.title: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
items.summary:
Like Russell Brand, my father was put on a pedestal by the media, despite a history of troubling, misogynistic comments. Meanwhile, my mother suffered through years of appalling treatment

Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear.

I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her.

items.title: Anthropic’s early birds are getting very rich
items.summary:
Anthropic signage at the Morgan Stanley headquarters in New York on November 18, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

Americans have debated, derided, praised, and protested the frontier AI labs. But they’ve never been able to directly own a piece of one…until tomorrow at 9 am.

That’s when Anthropic, developer of the chatbot Claude, is expected to go public at a valuation of more than $1 trillion . That would immediately rank the almost-six-year-old lab among the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies — up there with the likes of Walmart and JPMorgan Chase.

It’s a major public test of what investors think Anthropic is worth, at a moment when a lot of people — policymakers, regulators, and technologists among them — are questioning the economic and social value of the AI industry. AI stocks have been shaky lately, and many of the new congressional Democrats have promised to take a tougher stance toward data centers and related technology. 

But you wouldn’t know it from the hype around the IPO, which is on track to become one of the largest ever. Anthropic initially set a price range of $70 to $78 a share, then reportedly revised the offering at $83 per share as demand surged far beyond the number of shares available. 

Investors are apparently betting that Anthropic has more growing to do. For ordinary buyers, that represents a chance to share in a company whose technology could cost us our jobs…
items.t: Anthropic’s early birds are getting very rich

items.title: Trump’s looming nominations crunch
items.summary:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) in the US Capitol Building on November 10, 2026. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images 

This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .

Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is running out of time to get his nominees confirmed. 

What’s happening? On Wednesday, outgoing Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy blocked Trump’s nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, Jim O’Neill, from confirmation. And last night, the White House pulled another nominee, would-be FDA commissioner Heidi Overton, from consideration ahead of a Wednesday committee vote. 

Both come at the worst possible time for Trump, who’s facing a dwindling legislative calendar with a Republican Senate majority on its way out. 

Cassidy, a physician, chairs the Senate health committee, which is responsible for approving both nominations before they go to the full Senate. On Tuesday evening, he wrote in a social media post that “unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”

What’s the context? A new Congress will be sworn in on January 3, in about a month and a half, and Democrats will hold sizable majorities in both chambers.

In reality, though, the Senate has less time than that to deal with new nominations: Not only are the holidays approaching, but Congress has other big-ticket priorities on its plate, including heading off another government shutdown and potential deals on…

items.title: The router that took down America’s antique air traffic system, explained
items.summary:
A traveler at Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Austin, Texas, on November 16, 2026. | Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images 

Last week — on Friday the 13th, of all days — everyone became hyperaware of how fragile our air infrastructure is. For four hours and 21 minutes, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, grounding all flights. 

Tens of thousands of flights were impacted, even more people were stuck at airports, and theories about the cause spread like wildfire. Then the Trump administration finger-pointing began. 

Eventually, however, the truth came out: The grounding wasn’t the result of a cyberattack, some kind of AI incident, or something even stranger. Instead, it was routine — though maybe ill-considered — maintenance gone awry. 

Even with the mystery solved, though, the fact that so many flights were grounded over what was revealed to be a problem with a router somewhere in Arkansas is troubling the American public in a real way. 

So how did it all go down? Darryl Campbell writes about aviation for The Verge, and he talked with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about how one router brought down the entire aviation system, why it’s likely to happen again, and what we could do to stop it. 

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .

items.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
items.summary:
Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon

Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place (BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November).

The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies.

items.t: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter

items.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
items.summary:
A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything

The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.”

It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”.

items.title: The US helped the world rein in nuclear weapons. Could it do the same for AI?
items.summary:
The unfinished work of nuclear governance offers an important lesson for those struggling with the risk of AI now: learning to live with a dangerous technology is not the same as eliminating its threat.  | Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto/Getty Images 

When Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker talks about the threat of artificial intelligence, he offers an increasingly common point of comparison: it is a danger “on the level of nuclear weapons.” 

The comparison is not far-fetched. If the international community found ways to constrain a potentially catastrophic technology once before, perhaps those arrangements can help us constrain another. 

The trouble is that while nuclear nonproliferation may be a useful framework for thinking about regulating AI, it isn’t necessarily a good one. Not because the technologies are too different, but because nuclear nonproliferation hasn’t actually freed us from the prospect of nuclear war. 

Nevertheless, the unfinished work of nuclear governance offers an important lesson for those struggling with the risk of AI now: learning to live with a dangerous technology is not the same as eliminating its threat. 

What we might be able to do, however, is eliminate uncertainty about who’s building AI, what AI is capable of, and when AI puts people at risk. The US has done exactly that with nuclear weapons by declassifying information about the size and condition of its own arsenal, encouraging other nuclear powers to do the same.

Prioritizing transparency about AI wouldn’t eliminate the dangers altogether, but it might help us move forward more collectively as we…
items.t: The US helped the world rein in nuclear weapons. Could it do the same for AI?

items.title: Who gets to decide Venezuela’s future?
items.summary:
In the days after the military operation that ousted Nicolás Maduro , a poll from the Caracas‑based firm Meganálisis showed that 92 percent of Venezuelans were grateful to President Donald Trump for removing Maduro and that 90 percent wanted the US as Venezuela’s main ally. During the months since, the US has been heavily involved in shaping Venezuela’s future. But some key reforms are moving slower than Venezuelans hoped for. 

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a three-step plan for US intervention in Venezuela : stability, recovery, and a transition to democracy. While plans for political reforms and democratic elections in Venezuela are moving slowly, the designs for who controls its oil have been moving fast. The US recently announced an agreement with Venezuela as “ the biggest oil deal in world history .” 

As Venezuelans hold out hope that the final step in Rubio’s plan, a transition to democracy, will still materialize, support among Venezuelans for Trump appears to be slipping. According to a new Meganálisis poll, 83 percent of Venezuelans don’t believe Trump wants what is best for their countr y. As voices grow louder from opposition leaders like Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado to jumpstart democratic processes, pressure on the US is mounting to make good on their promise.

items.title: Beijing has three priorities at the Shenzhen summit – a China expert explains
items.summary:
China is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit for the third time in the past 25 years. The gathering in Shenzhen will see the leaders of the US, China and Russia sit down together for a formal three-way meeting for the first time in history.

But what does China want from the summit? I see it as having three main priorities. First is to consolidate its position as one of the world’s most important diplomatic hubs. Second is to set out its vision for a new global order.

And third is to take advantage of favourable geopolitical conditions, primarily brought about by US setbacks in Iran and Russia’s quagmire in Ukraine, to adjust the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow.

1. A diplomatic hub

Hosting national leaders and other high-level officials has become a key feature of Chinese diplomacy in recent years. President Xi Jinping has welcomed over 25 world leaders to China so far in 2026. These include Canada’s Mark Carney, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez and the UK’s former prime minister, Keir Starmer.

Beijing’s push to become a key diplomatic convener is a notable break from earlier forms of Chinese diplomacy. In the 2010s, the assertive and confrontational approach of Chinese officials on the…
items.t: Beijing has three priorities at the Shenzhen summit – a China expert explains

items.title: A perfect storm is descending on the AI industry
items.summary:
An aerial view of a 33 megawatt data center with closed-loop cooling system on April 14, 2026 in Vernon, California. | Mario Tama/Getty Images 

The stock market is set to christen a new trillion-dollar company on Wednesday, as the AI juggernaut Anthropic goes public.

Key takeaways 

Fears of an AI market crash are growing, with tech stocks sliding sharply since June.

The AI industry is spending far more on infrastructure than it earns, and cheaper “good enough” models threaten the profits of frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.

Three recent shocks have made things worse.

The boom may survive, but AI companies can no longer count on governments deferring to them or markets cheering them on. 

The IPO should have been the crowning triumph of the AI boom — a testament to the technology’s mind-bending commercial value, which enabled a seven-person startup to become a world-conquering juggernaut in five short years.

But all is not well with Silicon Valley. Even as investors scramble to claim a piece of our future God-emperor, Claude Opus 5,000 ( hallowed be his name! ), fears of an AI market crash are building. 

Since June, tech stocks have taken a beating, with one generative AI ETF shedding 35 percent of its value. Over the same period, the Philadelphia semiconductor index — a rough gauge of the chip industry’s value — fell by more than one-third.

The sell-off gained steam in recent weeks, as Republicans lost key elections to AI-skeptical Democrats — and Nvidia lost its longtime CEO to a geopolitically explosive sex scandal, a leadership change that has…

Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump are meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.

The meeting is no doubt unusual – a very rare opportunity for the leaders of the world’s three major powers to exchange views directly on major global issues.

It’s drawn comparisons to the Yalta conference of 1945, when US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian leader Joseph Stalin met to divide the world into spheres of influence after the second world war.

But this is no Yalta 2.0. Nor is the Shenzhen summit an isolated episode. In May this year, Xi hosted back-to-back visits by Trump and Putin to Beijing. Trump reciprocated by hosting Xi in Washington in September, and met with Putin in Alaska last year.

Taken together, these developments signal a broader shift away from the post-Cold War emphasis on global institutions and multilateral consultations toward a more personalised form of great power management.

items.title: The case for new Democratic leadership
items.summary:
Members of Democratic leadership in the House and Senate Democratic walk out of the US Capitol on May 21, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images 

After historic wins in the midterm elections, Democrats now have to decide who will lead their new majorities in the House and the Senate. The House race is expected to be a formality, with current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries as the sole declared candidate for House speaker. 

The Senate race, however, is shaping up to be more interesting: In the upper chamber, current minority leader Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who argues that Senate Democrats need new leadership to meet the demands of voters who delivered them a majority.

“The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual,” Van Hollen said . “And to do that, I think we need new leadership.” 

Van Hollen is also the favored candidate of the party’s progressive faction, many members of which have soured on Schumer. Corbin Trent, a former communications director for Rep. He also argues that Democrats should embrace a more proactive style of governing that harkens back to the New Deal era.

items.t: The case for new Democratic leadership

items.title: When do we start worrying about all these outages?
items.summary:
Have you tried to take a flight in the last week? What about check your email , your bank balance , your Apple account ? (Or, for a select few of us, your top-secret internal spy agency network ?)

If you have, you might have noticed that some or all of those services didn’t work as expected. First, Microsoft’s cloud programs, such as Outlook, went down late last week. Then, all of the planes were grounded on Friday. And this week, we had to deal with the bank outages, a separate United Airlines-specific outage, the Apple outage, and the NSA communications outage. 

As of this writing, most of these issues have now been ironed out, at least for the time being, and there’s no indication that any of them were cyberattacks or otherwise malicious. But whatever the reasons, it sure feels like there have been a lot more outages this week and last than in a usual seven-day stretch. 

To get to the bottom of it — hopefully before something else shorts out — the Today, Explained team spoke with Lily Hay Newman , a senior writer at WIRED who covers hacking, information security, and digital privacy. 

She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about why it took Microsoft so long to get Outlook back on its feet, all of the other recent outages we’ve suffered, and whether it’s as unprecedented as it feels in the moment. Plus, she explains how AI is causing a broader “vulnepocalypse” (or “ Vulnageddon ”), even if it’s not specifically the culprit of all of our current outages.

items.title: Voyager 1 is about to reach a mind-bending milestone
items.summary:
An artist’s rendering of the Voyager approaching Saturn, circa the late 1970s. | Space Fronteirs/Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

Shortly after 5 am ET tomorrow morning, while much of the East Coast is still in bed, Voyager 1 will cross a threshold that’s kind of hard to comprehend.

The 49-year-old spacecraft will reach a point about 16 billion miles from Earth — the distance that light travels in 24 hours. 

Scientists call that unit a light-day. And while it’s not a particularly meaningful scientific measurement, it’s a pretty good opportunity to marvel at how far Voyager has voyaged.

The craft first set out in 1977 to explore our solar system’s outer planets, including Jupiter and Saturn. It flew past both planets, snapping photos of their surfaces and making several big discoveries , before reaching interstellar space in 2012. 

Today, both Voyager and its sister, Voyager 2, remain part of an active NASA mission measuring the gases and magnetic field outside the Sun’s protective magnetic bubble. Both spacecraft also famously carry identical copies of the so-called Golden Record, which contains images and recordings meant to introduce humanity to passing aliens. That means Voyager isn’t just interesting as a live experiment or a souvenir of America’s 1970s space ambitions — but as an attempted self-portrait of human civilization.

items.title: How to be a good-enough home cook

Editor’s note, November 17, 2026, 5 pm ET : This story is being republished for the holiday season. It was originally published in 2022. 

The running gag among anyone who’s ever tasted a morsel of my cooking is that I must not know what salt is. It’s a fair critique: I somehow manage to overcook and under-season virtually every meal I prepare. I’m clumsy and unconfident with a knife and prefer to prepare most foods in a microwave or Instant Pot. 

Whipping up a meal is sometimes a nutritional puzzle. If all you’re working with at the moment are tortillas, frozen broccoli, and canned beans, you (like me) may struggle to conjure up something decent to eat. 

Cooking can also feel like a chore. Parents not only have to feed themselves, but send their kids off to school with packed lunches and prepare snacks and dinner after that. One recipe can dirty up a whole sink’s worth of dishes. 

Just like any other life skill , cooking is one that requires practice. “Eating is such a human thing — that’s the first skill we learn,” says Jess Dang , the founder of the online meal planning service Cook Smarts . “People think if I know how to eat, I must be able to know how to cook too, but they’re totally separate things.” If you weren’t taught the basics of cooking from school or a loved one, you might feel your time in the kitchen is doomed; if you’re already stretched thin financially and time-wise, cooking can feel like a fraught endeavor. However, with a few foundational skills and pantry staples, even the most beginner home chefs can whip up some delicious meals in no time at all.…
items.t: How to be a good-enough home cook

items.title: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era
items.summary:
James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

items.title: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop
items.summary:
On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia.

Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia.

The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices.

Regional flavour

Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together).

While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English.

By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual.
